speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief report to the house on the meeting of the Canada-United States joint committee on trade and economic affairs which took place in Washington yesterday and the day before.
The United States was represented by Hon. Dean Rusk, Secretary of State; Hon. George W. Ball, under secretary of state for economic affairs; Hon. Douglas Dillon, Secretary of the Treasury; Hon. Henry R. Fowler, under secretary of the treasury; Hon. Luther H. Hodges, Secretary of Commerce; Hon. Stewart H. Udall, Secretary of the Interior, and Hon. Orville L. Freeman, Secretary of Agriculture. The United States delegation also included Hon. George C. McGovern, coordinator of the food for peace program.
The Canadian government was represented by my colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Agriculture, and myself. The Canadian delegation also included the under secretary of state for external affairs, Mr. N. A. Robertson, the Canadian ambassador to the United States, Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, and officials of the various departments.
This was the first meeting of the committee since the new United States administration took office. The Canadian ministers were anxious that the United States members 90205-6-190
should view individual problems in the context of the entire framework of economic relations between our two countries. Accordingly we took the occasion to review at some length the Canadian economic situation and to show which features of our situation were common to both countries and which features were different. Both countries, for example, have shared the same experience of a slowing down of growth and of high levels of unemployment. We reviewed together the measures both countries had taken to stimulate greater economic activity, and we were agreed that an expansion of growth would result.
Both countries have had special problems related to the balance of payments. In this respect, however, our problems in Canada have been somewhat different from those of the United States. It was valuable to have an opportunity at this meeting to explain these differences to our United States colleagues and to analyse features of our balance of payments along the lines I followed in this house when introducing the supplementary budget last December.
The United States balance of payments was examined in the context of the world financial situation. As hon. members are aware, there have been serious problems of international imbalance associated with short term capital movements. Now that the major currencies are convertible and capital moves more freely it is clear that the industrial countries of western Europe and North America will have to continue and improve their methods of consultation about the economic policies of individual countries as they may affect others. We believe that the organization for economic co-operation and development will provide a very useful forum for such consultation.
It was clear from our discussions this week that the members of the committee are in broad agreement that the 1960's will produce new and rather different problems from those both countries have faced in the past. The great expansion of the economies of the western European countries is presenting a competitive challenge to both the United States and Canada. We found that the United States side attached great importance, as we do ourselves, to ensuring that the development of regional trading groups and any arrangements between them do not restrict the traditional access of North American exports

Canada-U.S. Trade Committee to the markets of western Europe. The committee agreed, especially, that in the current tariff negotiations at Geneva the six countries of the common market should assure that access. Canadian ministers were particularly gratified to learn that the new administration would continue to co-operate closely with Canada in pressing the Six for a satisfactory settlement in GATT with respect to trade in agricultural products.
The relations of Canada and the United States with the Six and the Seven will be of the greatest importance in the years to come. The establishment of the new O.E.C.D. will provide a framework in which Canada, the United States and their European partners will be able to examine and discuss each other's policies with respect not only to trade and economic matters but also to the vital task of assisting the less developed countries. I was able to report to my United States colleagues that Canada was the first country to complete parliamentary approval of the O.E.C.D. convention, having done so by unanimous vote of both houses, and Canada is now in a position to ratify.
In the meetings this year special attention was also given to the problems facing the underdeveloped countries. I am confident that the long-standing co-operation between the two countries in this field will be continued and indeed strengthened. I was struck by the conviction within the committee that the developed countries, particularly those with surpluses to invest abroad, must find satisfactory and equitable means to respond to the needs of the developing countries, and above all defeat the threat of poverty and starvation in so many parts of the world.
Ideas and actions, some of which are developing and others of which are planned in connection with the use of food to help raise levels of consumption and standards of nutrition were discussed, including the latest developments in the United States food for peace program. The United States indicated support for multilateral arrangements such as the Canadian proposal for a world food bank, which they had joined in sponsoring before the United Nations general assembly last October .This proposal is at present being given detailed study by FAO and it is expected that recommendations for appropriate action by governments will be forthcoming later this year. Other points relating to agreement on the continuation of close consultations to ensure that present and potential commercial markets for food products are not disrupted are recorded in the communique and I need not repeat these at length. I may say, however, that Canadian ministers were very pleased to receive from the new administration such a clear undertaking in this regard.


The committee also discussed a number of matters less general in scope but of direct importance to trade and economic relations between our two countries. Measures taken by Canada since our last meeting were reviewed. In this regard I had the opportunity to give a full explanation of the proposals put before parliament in the supplementary budget, notably its tariff and tax provisions. As a result of our useful discussions on this subject, I believe our United States colleagues have a full understanding of these proposals.
Canadian ministers raised a number of points bearing on our exports to the United States, such as import restrictions on agricultural products and on lead and zinc, certain customs problems, and the difficulties raised for Canada by the United States export subsidy on cotton manufactures. As a result of these exchanges of view I believe the United States members of the committee should have no doubt about the difficulties faced by Canadian exporters as a result of United States policies in these fields.
This meeting of the joint committee provided a welcome opportunity for Canadian ministers and the new United States secretaries to meet each other and gain a clear understanding of points of view in both countries. This meeting, like previous meetings of the committee, was characterized by the utmost frankness and friendliness.
Following the meeting my colleagues and I had the honour of being invited to call on the President with whom we had a most interesting talk. This meeting afforded an opportunity for further discussion of trade and economic questions and of the visit of the President and Mrs. Kennedy to Ottawa, which is awaited by Canadians with pleasant anticipation.
Mr. Speaker, may I table for the information of the house a copy of the communique which was issued at the conclusion of the committee meetings. If it is the wish of hon. members perhaps it could be printed as an appendix to today's Hansard.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members will have listened with interest to the minister's statement. Although we have not had the advantage of seeing the communique which presumably was issued yesterday and which has now been tabled, nevertheless from the minister's statement

and from press reports-especially, I may add, the latter-we are able to get a picture of the meetings that have just taken place in Washington.
The minister in introducing his statement said it had been decided that the individual national problems between the two countries would be considered within the framework of international economic policy. It is perfectly clear from the minister's statement that more attention was given to the framework than to the picture, because the communique deals almost entirely with international economic policies and the views of the two governments in respect of them.
In so far as the minister's statement dealing with these matters is concerned, it is satisfactory to note that the two governments are in general agreement on the usefulness of O.E.C.D., which is apparently to be pretty carefully restricted to consultative matters on the desirability of further progress being made in the discussions now going on through GATT and the desirability of co-ordinating policies in respect of international agricultural disposal matters. It is all to the good that the two governments should try to reach agreement on these matters, and that agreement, though in very general terms, seems to find expression in the communique so far as we can judge from the minister's statement.
The minister made little reference to individual problems between the two countries. However, we learned from the press that they had come up and the minister indeed did mention that fact, and that there was an exchange of views in regard to them. I would have hoped that there would be no hesitation on the part of the Canadian representatives to take up with the United States governmental representatives such questions as national oil policy, the United States policy on base metals and the policy of that country in giving additional contracts at this time to their uranium producers when only a year ago they told us there was a surplus of uranium and that was why they had to refuse to take up their options on our uranium.
I would have hoped, Mr. Speaker, that the government would make the position of Canada perfectly clear in these matters. We learned from the press-the minister did not confirm the fact this afternoon, though he did mention it-that the United States ministers challenged the assertion that the new class or kind provisions did nothing to contravene Canada's obligations under GATT, thereby confirming the view that we on this side take about these provisions.

Mr. Speaker, the minister said in his statement there was broad agreement between Canada and the United States that the 1960's would produce new problems. I think that is a conclusion that we all were aware of in advance. The minister has outlined a number of problems, but there is no indication in his statement that there has been any conclusion as to the solution for those problems. However, the minister did say that in dealing with the inner six, Canada and the United States would continue to co-operate in pressing on the inner six the need for a satisfactory settlement with regard to agricultural products being imported into that area. We can only hope that this pressure will be successful. Instead of a forward step in obtaining extra markets or increased markets for our products, what it really means is just holding the line.
The minister went on to talk at some length about the problems and the possibilities of expanded sales of Canadian food products and the whole question of economic assistance. There seemed to be no agreement following these discussions. There seems to be no agreement that Canada will have a peace corps. We ourselves are going to do nothing to increase economic assistance by way of a greater provision of food products. There was an assurance from the United States, which we are glad to receive, that that country will not interfere with our normal commercial markets for food products. That leaves beyond decision the whole field of non-commercial markets into which the United States has moved in a very big way.
The minister said that after speaking to the Americans he has come to the conclusion that they have a full understanding of Canada's tariff proposals. I am not sure

Canada-XJ.S. Trade Committee whether this is good or bad, Mr. Speaker. It might result in some very severe retaliation. I am sure the Americans will thank the minister for his information and instruction.
There has been no settlement of many outstanding problems such as the whole question of the disposal by the United States of its agricultural surpluses in non-commercial markets, the problem of exports of oil from Canada and so on. No doubt there was a very welcome exchange of ideas. The minister talked of a friendly and frank approach. The minister and his colleagues have had so many laudable things to say about the new United States administration that we had really hoped they would have been able to achieve more concrete results.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the opposition seem to be very hard to please this afternoon, and I am hoping they will not receive my announcement in such a manner. I am pleased to announce the appointment of Mr. H. F. Feaver as Canada's first ambassador to Tunisia. Direct diplomatic relations have, of course, existed between Tunisia and Canada since September 9, 1957, when His Excellency Mongi Slim, presented his credentials as first ambassador of Tunisia to Canada. The appointment of Mr. Feaver will complete the diplomatic connection with a country whose role in international affairs is one of great and growing importance and with which we have enjoyed particularly effective co-operation at the United Nations. As a matter of fact, Tunisia has made an enviable reputation as a member of the security council during the current year.
Hon. members will recall that Mr. Feaver's appointment as ambassador to Switzerland was announced last month. His present appointment to Tunisia will mean that he will concurrently represent Canada in that country as well. Although his normal residence will be in Berne, he will pay frequent visits to Tunisia.
Mr. Feaver, a native of Nova Scotia, has had a long and distinguished career with the Department of External Affairs both at home and abroad since 1930. He has served in Washington, Tokyo, London and The Hague. He was Canadian minister to Denmark from 1954 to 1956 and Canadian ambassador there from 1956 until his return to Ottawa in August, 1958, where he has since been chief of protocol.
At the same time I should like to announce that for some time it has been the government's hope that it would be possible to establish some Canadian diplomatic representation in Iraq. Discussions to this end have recently been taking place with the Iraqi government. I am pleased to inform the house that it is the government's intention to accredit to Baghdad Mr. Paul Andre Beaulieu, Q.C., the Canadian ambassador to Lebanon. Under this

dual accreditation arrangement, Mr. Beaulieu will continue to maintain his residence in Beirut but will, of course, be in a position to pay regular and frequent visits to Baghdad as well.
Mr. Beaulieu was born in Outremont, Quebec, was educated in Montreal and practised law there prior to the war. He joined the Department of External Affairs in 1940 and has since seen service in Washington, Paris, London and Boston, where he was consul from 1949 to 1951. He was originally appointed charge d'affaires of the Canadian legation in Lebanon in April, 1958, and became ambassador there in October, 1958, when the status of the mission was raised to embassy.
Mr. Beaulieu's appointment will demonstrate Canada's recognition of the increasingly important role which Iraq is playing in international affairs and the growing need for closer relations between our two countries. This appointment also is one of several, of which the Sudan, I hope, will be another, intended to strengthen Canada's representation in Asia and Africa.

Now we are told he is to be given the additional assignment of serving as our representative in Tunisia. It is appropriate that Canada should be among those countries to have representation in Tunisia because of the efforts made by Canada toward the admission of Tunisia into the United Nations and the acquiring by her of the status of a self-governing nation.
Mr. Feaver is a distinguished public servant who has represented Canada abroad with distinction on several occasions. He has performed notable and valuable services to his country in the Department of External Affairs here in Ottawa.
The appointment of Mr. Paul Beaulieu as our ambassador to Iraq has fulfilled an intention which the minister from time to time indicated to the house the government had in mind. The minister will recall that on several occasions I asked him if there was any likelihood of an appointment being made by Canada to Iraq by way of establishing a Canadian mission there. The minister replied that consideration was being given to this matter. It is significant that the government of Iraq announced the day before yesterday that it had decided to establish a diplomatic mission in Canada. One wonders why the announcements were not simultaneous. I do not say this by way of criticism, but it is rather

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I wish to advise the house that the terms of a new postal convention between Canada and the United States will come into effect on July 1 of this year. This convention replaces one which has been in existence since 1922. The new agreement between our two administrations reviews the exchange of mails between our countries in the light of present conditions and brings up to date informal understandings arrived at over the years.
Of major interest, particularly to Canadian newspaper and periodical publishers, is the inclusion in the new convention of an article stipulating that second class mail in each country addressed for delivery in the other shall be chargeable at a rate not less than the lowest international postage rate in effect for such printed matter. This means, in effect, that postage rates on United States newspapers and periodicals entering Canada will be substantially increased. The higher rate also applies to Canadian publications mailed to the United States, but in view of the relatively small volume of this type of mail it should have comparatively little adverse effect on Canadian publishers.
I might just mention in this connection that about 150 copies of United States publications come to Canada for every copy of a Canadian publication going to the United States. As an illustration, the rate on a typical monthly magazine mailed in the United States for Canada will increase from about 6 cents per pound to a minimum of a little over 8 cents per pound.

Canada-U.S. Postal Convention
The United States has also announced its intention to make rate changes on certain other types of mail addressed to Canada effective July 1. Generally these changes are designed to apply the same rates on such mail as exist for domestic United States mail. No such changes are to be made in Canada, since in the categories concerned the domestic postage rate already applies to mail addressed to the United States.
Under the new convention the service on unpaid or insufficiently prepaid letters and postcards originating in the United States will be improved, as henceforth all such mail will be forwarded promptly rated double deficiency instead of being delayed at origin for the missing postage. Such a practice has been followed in Canada for some time. Also, the maximum weight of parcels exchanged between the two countries will be increased from 15 to 25 pounds and the maximum indemnity for the loss of a registered article increased from $25 to $100. The new scale of weights for parcel post to the United States will, of course, require a revision of parcel post rates on such mail, and this is currently under way.
The convention also deals with a variety of technical postal questions affecting the service between both countries. I should like to express my appreciation here for the cooperative way in which United States postal officials worked with us on the drafting of this convention from the time the project was first suggested by the Canadian Post Office Department over a year ago.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I noticed that the Postmaster General read the statement rather rapidly. I did not hear any reference to the royal commission which was presided over by Mr. O'Leary. Perhaps before the Postmaster General made any change in postal rates between the United States and Canada, he should have waited for the report of the royal commission, or perhaps he should have attended before that commission as a witness.
The postal rates between the United States and Canada seem to be about the same both ways, even after these changes. If the purpose of these changes was to limit the number of United States periodicals or magazines entering Canada, I do not believe they will have any effect at all. The only result will be to impose a kind of indirect tax on the periodicals and magazines. Another result of this change will be to increase the cost of living in Canada as well as in the United States.
In conclusion I should like to say I believe the Postmaster General should have awaited the report of the royal commission before making these changes.

speechtext:
We welcome this announcement the result of which is, in effect, an amelioration of the competition of Canadian publishers with United States publishers, although it is difficult to know just how significant this will be. One of the points about this announcement, and it is not a vitally important one but it is peculiar, is that the whole idea was released in the United States on March 6. Despite the fact that we have had parliamentary questions centring on this area since that time, we have had to wait until today for this announcement. There was a full news report covering this change in the United States yesterday, so the people of the United States seem to have had this information when Canadians did not. I was wondering whether, in any liaison the minister might have with United States officials in the future, he could see that we get the same break the United States does in terms of information.
The other point that is not at all clear from the statement, and the minister might clarify this right now, is whether United States publications mailed in Canada are going to be affected by this agreement. It is apparent that publications mailed into Canada are going to be affected, but we are given no information about whether or not the ones mailed in Canada will be affected.
The next point is that the minister has not given us any indication as to whether Canada is going to get a share of the greater revenues that will accrue to the United States postal authorities for handling these periodicals that come into Canada. If the disparity is, as the minister says, 150 to 1, then it is obvious the Canadian post office is going to continue to subsidize United States publications, that is unless some form of rebate is a part of this agreement. It would have been welcome to know whether or not the minister made any gains in that particular field.

It was available to any hon. member of the house today.
It was not even my intention to refer to it in the house. speechtext:
Standing order 40 (1) confirms what the Minister of Finance has indicated. I believe this standing order is now in the

form in which it was established only in 1955, when a new practice was adopted in this respect. This standing order says:
(1)	Any return, report or other paper required to be laid before the house in accordance with any act of parliament or in pursuance of any resolution or standing order of this house may be deposited with the Clerk of the house on any sitting day, and such return, report or other paper shall be deemed for all purposes to have been presented to or laid before the house.
(2)	A record of any such return, report or other paper so deposited shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings of the same day.
It is clear, of course, that if there is any failure to observe the rules or orders of the house it is a breach of the privileges of the house which entitles an hon. member to complain. However, from what has been said I do not see any complaint that this rule has not been observed. As the matter has been amply discussed, unless somebody wishes to assert that the rule has not been observed and that therefore a breach of privilege arises, I think we might consider the matter closed.

I have ascertained that the practice in the Clerk's office is not to release documents which are tabled in accordance with the rule which I read, standing order 40, until 2.30 p.m. The logic behind this is that the rule permits such documents to be tabled by depositing them with the Clerk of the house on any sitting day. By perhaps an excess of caution the office of the house which receives these documents in the name of the Clerk does not consider that they have been received on a sitting day until the house actually sits. Therefore the authority to the distribution office of the house to distribute them is not given until that time. That is the explanation of part of the point which the Leader of the Opposition was making.

Mr. Speaker, following the reference earlier this afternoon to this matter, the Leader of the Opposition sent over to me a copy of the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, March 15, 1961. The article, which bears the caption "By Bruce Phillips, Southam News Services" is undoubtedly a review or report upon the report of the governor of the bank which became available, as you have indicated, at 2.30 this afternoon. That was the time at which the tabling became effective, as you have now said and was the time appointed for its release by members of the press gallery or the press to whom it was made available yesterday. Therefore there can be no doubt that the news report on the report of the governor of the bank did appear in this edition of the Ottawa Citizen dated Wednesday, March 15.
I then caused inquiry to be made at the offices of the Ottawa Citizen to determine at what time this edition of the Ottawa Citizen was published. I am told that it was not published until 2.30 p.m. today. I am told further that the Citizen does not reach Ottawa newstands before 2.30 p.m.; that the Citizen is not delivered to any subscriber before 2.30 p.m., and that the embargo on the report was 2.30 p.m. I am further told that no copy of this newspaper could have come into the

hands of any persons expect those in the trade, that is to say representatives of the two Ottawa newspapers, before 2.30 p.m. today.
Mr. Speaker, I can only infer therefore that the copy in question could not have come into the hands of the Leader of the Opposition before 2.30 p.m., but if he tells us that a copy did come into his hands before 2.30 p.m. I think he owes it to the house to tell us how such a copy came into his hands before 2.30 p.m. today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    PRESS PUBLICATION OF BANK OF CANADA REPORT
speechtext:
I realize this is not an occasion for a debate, but I have two observations to make on the statement which has just been made by the Leader of the Opposition. First of all, the hon. gentleman regards it as a discourtesy to the house that copies of this report should have been made available to the press yesterday with a release date of 2.30 p.m. today, that being the time at which it became available to members of the House of Commons. We are being asked, apparently, to believe that this is something unusual. This is not unusual. It has been the practice followed with regard to these matters for years. It is the practice followed with respect to the budget; it is the

practice with respect to the estimates. There is no secret about this. It is a fact that the contents of the budget speech are made known to the press, and that has been the practice for many years. It was the practice when the Leader of the Opposition was a member of the government.

subtopic: MR. PEARSON    PRESS PUBLICATION OF BANK OF CANADA REPORT
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. PEARSON    PRESS PUBLICATION OF BANK OF CANADA REPORT
speechtext:
It is true, and it is useless for the Leader of the Opposition to deny that, because we have simply followed with respect to these various matters -the budget, the estimates and other matters -a practice which was well established before we came into office.
My second observation is that apparently the Leader of the Opposition is not aware of the nature of the business we shall be dealing with for the rest of the afternoon. We are not to be debating financial resolutions. We will have before us the second reading of the bill to amend the Income Tax Act, and what relevance the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada has to the second reading of particular amendments to the Income Tax Act is a conundrum which apparently only the Leader of the Opposition can explain.

subtopic: MR. PEARSON    PRESS PUBLICATION OF BANK OF CANADA REPORT
speechtext:
I have perhaps allowed the discussion on this question of privilege to go farther than usual before determining whether it is a question of privilege, because I know the house is jealous of its right to receive information from the ministry before any outside body does, or at least on equal terms with any outside agency. It has been asserted that the practice which was followed in this particular case was in accordance with previous practice.
I do not myself recall any precedent for a question of privilege being sustained on the basis that the press had been given documents required to be tabled in the house for release at the time of tabling. However, there may be a question involved, and if hon. members wish to consider the matter for future occasions as a consequence of this complaint they are free to do so. As it stands at the moment, the complaint seems to be based on suggestions of discourtesy.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S ABSTENTION FROM VOTES
speechtext: In the light of the government's stated position on apartheid, I wonder if the Acting Prime Minister would care to explain to the house why Canada abstained from voting at the United Nations on a motion designed to end racial discrimination in South West Africa and place this area under United Nations trusteeship.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON CANADA'S ABSTENTION FROM VOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the facts in connection with this vote at the United Nations yesterday or the day before are as follows. The original draft resolution on South West Africa was introduced only on the morning of March 13. During the debate the resolution was extensively amended and in this altered form it was rushed to a vote that same afternoon. In the debate the Canadian delegation said that we would regret it if an immediate vote was taken on this important and complex resolution, since it had not been possible in the short time available to receive instructions. The delegation explained that if a vote were taken Canada would abstain solely-and this is the key to my answer-because there was inadequate time to receive instructions, and this would not indicate our position on the substance of the resolution. A similar stand was taken by several countries, including Ghana. All these countries urged that time be given to get instructions from their respective governments.
The resolution will now move from the committee stage to the plenary session of the United Nations and there, after due consideration in the department, instructions have been given for our delegation to vote for the resolution.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker; we have before us a particular bill that proposes certain quite definite amendments to the Income Tax Act. My point was that ten of the principles that are incorporated in the sections of the bill we are now considering may relate in a very direct way to the recommendations in the Bank of Canada report that became available to us only at 2.30 today. I say it is unfortunate, inasmuch as there is a direct relationship between these ten items contained in this bill, that we did not have this report at an earlier stage. This is the point I make, and I think it is a valid point.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I did say during the budget debate that I felt the contents of this income tax bill were likely to prove very meagre because a decision was made to present a baby budget before it was decided what might be available to put in it. Almost three months have elapsed since the introduction of the resolutions, and my view in that respect has not changed in the interval. I feel that instead of deriving much advantage from this bill a fair amount of damage has been done to this country in its present economic situation, and particularly in its relationships with foreign countries which traditionally have made substantial investments in Canada.
In the first place, I find that there is not too much here that is very trenchant or very vital. On the other hand, as a result of the talk in connection with this baby budget I

feel that there has been created abroad quite a blurred image in respect of intentions. I do not need to advance that as my own opinion. I was back for the baby budget. I was away of course, all through November, but I was back subsequent to the introduction of the baby budget. I think this confusion, rather than the direct effects of this bill, is causing great irratation and is doing Canada no noticeable good in other sections of the world.
There is a danger of creating wrong impressions, even though they may be inadvertently created. The minister must have sensed this danger. Certainly another hon. member of this house has already spoken on this point. I refer to the much admired hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith). He also has spent a great deal of time at the United Nations and in the country to the south. In the debate on the baby budget the hon. member confirmed the alarm that I have expressed, with regard to our contacts in the United States. They do not properly understand the intentions of this government with respect to investment and they are considerably alarmed about this matter.
I think the minister must have recognized this situation, because shortly after the presentation of the budget on December 20 he made a trip to New York city in order to try to allay some of the apprehensions that obviously existed in that financial centre. I report the impressions I received while I was down there. The minister went down to New York on January 18 and made a speech to the Canadian club. He had a very good audience. I had been to the Maple Leaf club a month before.
I want to produce evidence of the confusion between Canada's financial leaders. I refer to the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada. I wish to quote their remarks during speeches made in New York recently. I think these remarks are in juxtaposition to each other.
On January 18 the Minister of Finance in New York said this:
None of us is under any illusion that Canada could have achieved the rapid and broadly based expansion of our productive facilities during the last decade or more without these investments

from other countries. We fully recognize the great benefits which the economy has derived by reason of the new manufacturing and industrial techniques which have been introduced, and of the natural resources which have been developed.
That is what the senior financial official of this government said on January 18. However, a person to whom equal attention is paid in the United States is naturally the governor of the Bank of Canada. He made a speech in the same city on March 7 to the Economic club of New York. I wish to show how much confusion there is in the financial leadership of this country by quoting the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I ask hon. members of this house to compare his statement with that of the Minister of Finance. On March 7 Mr. Coyne said this:
The influence of the $9 billion of new foreign capital of one kind and another over the past decade-
The Minister of Finance had referred to the same decade.
-if anything has had rather adverse effects on stability of employment and costs of production.
Earlier this afternoon I asked whether or not the Minister of Finance had any opportunity to observe the reported increasing harmony between the federal reserve bank in the United States and President Kennedy and his new administration. If the minister did not have that opportunity during the last two days I hope he will continue to observe developments in that connection. At the present time there is an urgent need for the utmost harmony and co-operation in our monetary relations and we should have a better balance between the policies of the government as expressed by the Minister of Finance-and indeed some of the other ministers-and the policies espoused by the governor of the Bank of Canada.
I am not alone in expressing some alarm about the results of this baby budget. I suggest these things are not very important broadly to anybody's pocket book, but psychologically I think they are important. I am afraid difficulties have been caused that will affect employment. These difficulties cannot be compared to the actual amount of dollars and cents that may come to the treasury as a result of the tightening up of some of these measures with respect to withholding tax.
The minister need not take my word for some of these things. I know he has great regard for certain commentators who have also referred to his baby budget since February, 1961. I have never found the minister in any way minimizing the importance of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. In

It would be a pity if the growing sense of national consciousness so apparent in Canada today should become identified in the mind of Americans -or anyone else-with anti-Americanism. In truth, it would be much more than a pity: it would be an unmitigated disaster.

Canada's image abroad was becoming somewhat fuzzy, he said.
Surely this is not a reference to something which happened years ago. He is saying that Canada's image abroad is presently becoming fuzzy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member agree that he did not use the words "under this government" and that Mr. Bourke in his statement did not attribute responsibility to this government?

I do not intend to quibble. I could not possibly be the equal of the Minister of Finance when it comes to quibbling. But in the light of common sense, I am sure Canadians will realize that a man who addresses the public of Canada every year and who says that Canada's image abroad is becoming fuzzy is not referring to anything except what is happening in very recent times.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not the
point I was raising at all.

Now we shall find in this bill reference to some protection that is now being taken by the government in respect to some of the opportunities which have been available in recent years, I think on too generous a scale, to bond investors. I have pointed out in the last three years that the Minister of Finance has at times been almost desperate about borrowing money and that in consequence he has offered gimmicks

Income Tax Act
which have been exceedingly expensive in their net cost to the treasury. But everyone is aware of the eloquence of the Minister of Finance and the kind of language he uses when he is criticized with regard to such a matter. I refer to the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, March 19, 1959. It states:
William Benidickson, Liberal financial critic in the commons has suggested that the federal government is paying more for some of its borrowings than appears in interest rates.
This was written following a discussion with respect to the offering of a bond at a substantial discount and at a low nominal interest rate; if a person in a high income tax bracket acquired such bonds he would be doing so at a very substantial advantage. But this is the way in which we are treated when we offer, as is our duty, criticism of the Minister of Finance. I continue to quote from the Ottawa Citizen:
Mr. Fleming described Mr. Benidickson's statement on this point as "a shockingly misleading and inaccurate statement".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On a point of order, the hon. member is purporting to quote a passage from a newspaper of a particular date. If I recall correctly, what that article purports to do is to report a debate which took place in the House of Commons and I put forward for your consideration, Mr. Speaker, the point that when we are dealing with statements made in the course of debate in the House of Commons the proper course is to quote from Hansard itself and not to quote what newspapers have said in regard to the debate in the house.

On this point of order I suggest there is no such rule as that which the hon. member advances. I think the rule is that an hon. member is not permitted, if there is objection from his colleagues, to quote words which reflect upon this house. These words I have quoted reflect on no one but myself, and if I advance them and make some comment upon them I do not think any matter of privilege can be raised by any other member of the house. These words were used with respect to myself by the Minister of Finance and are reported in the Ottawa Citizen of March 19, 1959. They were used by a minister who intends to make amendments to the Income Tax Act to cover the very thing about which I at that time gave him a warning which he described as "a shocking, misleading and inaccurate statement" on my part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On that point of order, Mr. Speaker, the observations now made by the hon. member illustrate very well the reasons why it has been the practice and, if I am not mistaken, the rule of this house that when hon. members purport to

refer to statements made in the house they should quote from the record of this house and not attempt to read newspaper reports of our debates with all the interpretations that may appear in such newspaper reports. We have just had an illustration of the reason behind this practice and rule, because the hon. member has just directed his observations in that respect to something quite different from the point of my observations in the debate which he is now purporting to quote from a secondary source.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River wish to speak on the point of order?
I will hear your ruling, sir.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I can refer at once, of course, to Beauchesne, fourth edition, paragraph 157, where it is made clear that it is out of order to read extracts in a debate if they refer to other debates during the same session. That, however, does not apply in this case because I understand the hon. member is referring to a debate which took place in 1959.

Perhaps Your Honour might hear a word from me while you are perusing other authorities. Just to indicate that the Minister of Finance is following his usual style of being exceedingly technical and and obstructive when criticized, may I recall that some four or five weeks ago the Minister of Finance, reading from papers in his hand, was quoting from Hansard-may I speak hypothetically-that the year he was referring to was perhaps 1957. But what he actually was referring to was a requote which he delivered and which appeared in a subsequent edition of Hansard, and he could not provide the page. The house at that time had the courtesy to accept what the minister had said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before the hon. member makes assertions of that kind he should be prepared to give the page reference in the debates of this house, because he will not find anything there to corroborate or substantiate the silly accusations he has now made.
Well, this debate will afford me plenty of opportunity to go to the library after six o'clock, and I will quote later the hon. gentleman in full.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member should refer to the exact place in Hansard where this was done.

Is Your Honour making that ruling both with respect to the question I first raised and with respect to the later point raised by the Minister of Finance? I

know that after this second reading stage of the debate has been completed the bill will be further discussed in the committee of the whole and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Finance that this will be repeated, if desired, complete with Hansard page references.
I wish now to deal with one of the aims of the ten out of the 12 resolutions incorporated in this bill which refer to investment policy, particularly with respect to investments that originate abroad. One of the alleged features that prompted the government to embark on this course was that it would perhaps reduce what was generally regarded as an undesirable and rather substantial premium on the Canadian dollar in its relationship to the United States dollar.
Before we conclude this stage of the debate I should like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to explain to us why after three months the dollar is virtually at the point it was when the budget was introduced on December 20, although some temporary hope was raised that the budget itself had accomplished something along the line to which I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Acting Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Speaker, when he was in the chair and before you came into it, had to caution the hon. member several times for being out of order in going far beyond the limits of the present bill.
This is a bill to amend the Income Tax Act in certain definite particulars set out in the bill. This is not a resumption of the budget debate. There is nothing in this present bill that speaks of the exchange rate on the dollar. The hon. member in following this course is, in my submission, simply ignoring the previous rulings of the Speaker when he was in the chair earlier with respect to the hon. member's remarks, and the hon. gentleman is trespassing in fields other than those that are the proper subject for debate here. Surely on this motion we are debating the principle of Bill No. C-73, an act to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to that point of order and remind Your Honour that three months have elapsed since the Minister of Finance introduced his baby budget on December 20. In the meantime the minister has made in this country and elsewhere speeches in which he has attempted to explain to his audiences the purposes of the legislation which he introduced on December 20.
The minister invariably has said that one of the features he had in mind was the elimination of the large premium on the Canadian dollar in relation to its United States
Income Tax Act
counterpart. I say that if ten twelfths of the contents of this bill relate to matters that could have a direct effect upon the relationship of the Canadian and United States dollar and upon interest rates in this country and in particular in the country closest to us in our trading relationships, it is utterly fatuous for the Minister of Finance to suggest that Your Honour should narrow our discussion to the extent he outlined.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I was in
the chamber when Mr. Speaker made the suggested ruling previously and made comments relating to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson). I have been through this bill and I do not know if I could properly say that the contents of this bill would affect the rate of interest between Canada and the United States, and so on. I do not think that is what I am supposed to do. However, I do not see how that can be considered a principle of this bill; and of course on second reading we must relate our discussion to the principle of the bill. Once again I must suggest to the hon. member that he confine his remarks to the principle of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, at this time I challenge the Minister of Finance to say categorically that in the amendents proposed in this bill amending the Income Tax Act there was no intention on his part that its provisions should in any way have an effect upon the relationship of the Canadian and United States dollar.
The minister is apparently not going to answer on that point-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall be very pleased to make my remarks at this stage if that is the wish of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
If the
minister rises I shall have to advise the house that he will close the debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am prepared to do that, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is serious.
The hon. member is dealing with a point of order.
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member had not thought of it until the hon. member for Essex East suggested it.

To continue, Mr. Speaker, I insist, subject to your ruling and after a considerable amount of study, that since the introduction of the resolutions in December one of the basic purposes of the changes was a hope that there might be a narrowing of the gap between the United States dollar

Income Tax Act
and the Canadian dollar. The point I wish to raise at this time, however, is that this seems to be a very belated determination on the part of the government.
A few months earlier in May hon. members of the government did not seem to be the champions of a par or under par Canadian dollar. We have been unsuccessful in obtaining explanations and replies to questions we have raised concerning the fact that this same government through its agencies as recently as May last permitted $100 million to be utilized-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask you to deal with the way in which the hon. member is completely ignoring-yes, I say defying-your ruling. He is going completely outside the terms of this bill. The hon. member is making assertions now that I should like to debate on a proper occasion. The hon. gentleman is making assertions with no truth in them and I shall welcome the opportunity to debate them at an appropriate time. The rules of the house do not afford opportunity to any hon. member to debate matters of this nature in relation to this bill. The hon. member must be aware of that fact but he has been running over the line throughout his remarks all afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address myself to the point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: More obstruction.
The minister says, "More obstruction". I wish to say to the minister that that, of course, is an entirely unparliamentary remark.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A very true one.

The Minister of Finance strenuously persists in obstructing his own legislation and I am going to leave it at that. The hon. gentleman gets to his feet and raises points of order without producing any authority whatever. The mere assertion by the minister that something is out of order, in his judgment makes it out of order. The Minister of Finance in his great glory has to be reminded-
The Acling Speaker (Mr. Rea): Order. I wish the hon. member would speak to the point of order.
Mr. Speaker, the last remarks of the Minister of Finance are so offensive and provocative as to certainly justify some comment from us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Why don't you get on with your point of order?

We now hear from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture.
(Mr. Benidickson.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, we have listened to hon. members opposite raising points of order on this, that and the other thing throughout the entire session and we are getting pretty well fed up-
The Acling Speaker (Mr. Rea): Order. I am sorry but the Chair can hear only one point of order at a time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Why doesn't the hon. member speak to the point of order?

I appreciate the difficulty the Chair has with hon. members on the government benches who at every point resist any suggestion with which they disagree that is made by the opposition; and if hon. members opposite are irritated by our conduct, we want them to know that we in turn are irritated by their constant attempts to prevent us from expressing what we believe are correct opinions which we have a right to express in this house.
You have no opinions. Speak to the point of order.
Since we have had that contribution from the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) I propose to address myself to the question which Your Honour has asked-
It is about time.
Once again the hon. member for Wentworth makes a contribution. All that hon. gentleman is able to do is sit in his seat day after day-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Speak to the point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, you have asked the hon. member to address himself to the point of order and he refuses to do so.
He does not have one.

I propose to address myself to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, but when I hear these interruptions I propose, within the rules of the house, to deal with them. While the hon. gentleman is not one of those who offend in that particular, he might use his politeness and his good deportment as an example to some of his colleagues who apparently do not understand the meaning of these words.
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is raising a point which he feels has a very definite bearing on the proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act. I would refer Your Honour to clause 9 of the bill which deals with the exemption from the 15 per cent non-resident withholding tax at present granted for interest payable on

bonds of or guaranteed by the government of Canada. I would also refer Your Honour to page 8 of the bill, where we find the explanatory notes which deal with the repeal of the special 5 per cent rate of non-resident withholding tax on dividends paid to a nonresident corporation by its wholly owned subsidiary corporation in Canada, and then to clause 10 of the bill which seeks to impose a tax of 15 per cent on dividends paid by a resident of Canada after December 20, 1960, to a non-resident organization, and so forth. These particular provisions were suggested by the Minister of Finance to meet certain situations, and one of them may very well be the problem raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. Surely the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is justified in saying that the Minister of Finance has been driven to impose this particular form of taxation, namely the 15 per cent tax on dividends paid by a resident of Canada, and a tax on non-residents, because of the premium on the Canadian dollar. That may not be a sound argument but the hon. gentleman has the right to make it, and that is what he is doing. With great respect, I say that he has brought himself perfectly within the rules; otherwise, an hon. gentleman would not be allowed to interrogate the Minister of Finance on why he has resorted to these particular forms of taxation on non-residents or on residents with respect to United States holdings. In view of these particular provisions, surely it is restricting the form of debate to say that the statements made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River are out of order.
If there is some doubt in Your Honour's mind-and I do not think there is-and if Your Honour concludes he is satisfied, that would be the end of it so far as I am concerned because I think Your Honour is very fair in his rulings. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he is obviously concerned today; he is obviously irritated. If he wants his measures to pass why does he not let some more vigorous person such as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) do the objecting instead of himself? Every time the hon. gentleman rises in his place he delays the passage of the legislation by a week.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. If hon. members were to be allowed to discuss the effects of this bill, of course, they could go into very many realms of any type of financial situation. However, I do have the feeling that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was discussing fiscal policies in general. I think I should suggest to him that his remarks should be directed more to this bill to amend the Income Tax Act. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is an old
Income Tax Act
experienced parliamentarian and I am sure he can keep himself well within the bounds of this bill.

I thank you for your comments, sir. I do not in any way depart from my original statement.
Your Honour referred to effects. Surely, we are permitted to discuss the legislation. Generally we use the word "principles" at second reading stage but I was going to use the word "purposes". Surely, we are permitted to discuss the purposes of the legislation before us. I would hope that one of the major purposes of the bill, or one of the consequences of the legislation, would be a narrowing of the gap between the Canadian and the United States dollar. I think I have made my point adequately in that respect.
In addition, when one considers that ten twelfths of the legislation before us relates to amendments concerning foreign investments, I say that undoubtedly it is of great interest to us when we compare domestic interest rates and foreign interest rates. I hope that when we come to the individual clauses of the bill we shall have every opportunity to pursue this subject unless the minister, when he speaks, informs us that these are not among his purposes. I am not talking about effects because I do not think the effects have been very consequential.
I want to know whether one of the main purposes of the legislation is to have an influence upon the pattern of the spread between the Canadian and the United States dollar? When the minister replies I want him to tell us also the purpose of the legislation in relation to domestic interest rates. I am sure the minister will not be able to escape this, although I was astonished that he did not take advantage of the opportunity, three months after the introduction of this legislation, to bring this house and the country up to date on the results that have flowed from the introduction of this legislation.
When the minister replies I hope he will resolve the great concern that exists all across Canada as to the apparent lack of harmony between the monetary policies that may be initiated by the Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that anyone looking around the house would not suggest that we have an inspiring audience this afternoon. I hope to conclude my few brief remarks by six o'clock. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we apply ourselves steadily from now on to the business of this session, if we have the co-operation of the government and the opposition in the introduction of legislation, we would get through in good time. I suggest that we lose

Income Tax Act
a lot of time because of the repeated delays in dealing with legislation, that is, dealing with the resolution and then dropping it and going on with the bill later, and so on. If we could have the resolution introduced and then the bill so that we could continue the discussion in a logical and sequential manner we would gain a lot of time. I think a lot of time is lost by deferring these resolutions and bills from week to week and going at them in what I call a bits and bobs way. If we did that, Mr. Speaker-I want to sow a seed in the minds of hon. members before I say my little piece on this bill this afternoon-I am of the opinion we could satisfactorily and in a proper way deal with the business of this session so that it would conclude by June 15. I hope I have sown a seed in fertile soil.
Without doubt this is the type of bill on which the major discussion will take place on the various clauses. However, I have a few general observations to make. As I said before, I intend to be brief. I think it is quite safe to say that the principle of this bill is income taxation; it is the application of a section of the Income Tax Act. We in this group, Mr. Speaker, think that the Income Tax Act is the fairest form of taxation and is sound in principle but we have maintained throughout the years that the application of the principle is unfair and that we cannot by any stretch of the imagination say that the application is equitable to all classes of the Canadian people when one considers their varying economic circumstances.
For instance, in the application of the act there is no doubt that certain unfairness is caused by the fact that we do not have a capital gains tax in this country, which makes it possible for persons to make large gains and pay no income tax whatever. I am staying in order as carefully as I can, Mr. Speaker, and I simply want to mention that the fact we have no capital gains tax has caused unnecessary taxation on lower income groups. Then there are concessions to mining, smelting, oil and gas companies and no doubt those concessions make it necessary to continue a higher rate of taxation on the lower income groups.
We do not suggest for a minute that the state does not need the revenue to meet its expenses. However, before proceeding with my few brief remarks on the bill I wish on behalf of this group to urge the minister that when he comes to consider his budget he should give some consideration to the plight of the lower income groups who have had little consideration for some years as far as exemptions are concerned while the cost of living has been going up steadily. I think I have gone very little beyond the confines of what is in order at the present time, Mr. 
Speaker; and as the minister apparently is in a beneficent mood and is smiling I could not help reminding him of these things which we have repeated from time to time in former budget debates and on other occasions.
We are pleased to see in the bill now before us the exemption allowed for tuition fees. That exemption will be of assistance to a certain group of people who in many cases need it badly in order to carry on their education. We are glad to see the tax imposed on investment income from sources outside Canada because we think that is fair. We are glad to see the increase from $25,000 to $35,000 in the amount of income of companies subject to the 18 per cent tax. That should be of some assistance to smaller companies, particularly those that are having a difficult time to carry on. We are glad to see the repeal of the exemption with respect to the 15 per cent non-resident withholding tax. I have always been of the opinion that was somewhat unfair in relation to what resident Canadians, particularly those with small incomes, have to pay in taxation.
As I said before, our few comments will be made on the clauses concerned. However, on behalf of this group I urge the minister to give consideration to those sections of our society that have not received particular consideration in recent years. We know that the cost of living, the cost of operating the human machine, has gone up. We allow substantial depreciation on machinery and plant equipment but up to the present time we have not allowed sufficient for the deterioration and depreciation that occur in the human machine, and that is a matter of serious concern to the lower income groups. In relation to all our other economic difficulties and the plans that have been made to meet them, in my opinion this is a good time to consider a complete overhaul of the Income Tax Act in the light of the circumstances we face today. I have done my very best to remain in order, Mr. Speaker, and at this point I conclude my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister replies I would ask him to give us the reasons that were in his mind with respect to the provisions in clause 2, I believe it is, with regard to tuition fees. The minister has given relief in respect of tuition fees for 1961, which means that it will become effective from the middle of the academic term that began last September or October. I have had a considerable number of representations made to me, and I am sure other members have, by students and student organizations with respect to why the relief is not to be made effective from September or October of 1960 so as to
cover the whole of the academic year. When the minister replies I hope he will deal with that aspect.
Mr. Speaker, as it is about one minute before six may I call it six o'clock?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have made so very little progress this afternoon that I would ask the hon. member to speak until six o'clock. If the hon. member's remarks pertain to clauses of the bill, perhaps he would consider deferring them until we are in committee. I should be glad to make my reply now, Mr. Speaker, to expedite as far as possible moving the house into the committee stage.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Can the hon. member's remarks be made in committee?

My remarks are of a general nature and if I do not have leave to call it six o'clock I will continue. The bill before us now to amend the Income Tax Act arises out of the proposals put forward by the minister in his budget and was announced along with other measures as part of the government's plan to contribute toward a solution of the unemployment problem. It is in that light that I think we must discuss the principle of the bill. We can appreciate
Business of the House
the desire of the government to encourage increased Canadian ownership of our industry and increased participation of Canadian capital in the development of our natural resources. These are objectives which command our support but we must be careful that we do not attain these objectives at the expense of other objectives which are even more important. This bill is a part of the government's program to combat unemployment and surely that must be our No. 1 objective today because it is the paramount problem facing Canadians at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire from the house leader what the business is for tomorrow and Friday and will he also give some indication of what the business will be on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: As announced, tomorrow we will deal with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. With respect to Friday, and this may be subject to change, at the moment we are considering going ahead with supplementary estimates. On Monday and Tuesday we will likely have a supply motion but I will be definite about that tomorrow night.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
